prompt: `grep -i "money back"` over the help centre returned the article about returning a gift and missed the refund articles. Why?
hint: Look at what grep compares.

choices.text: grep matches exact characters, and only the gift article contains that exact string
choices.why: Right. The refund articles say refund, and a string search has no way to know that refund and money back describe the same thing.

choices.text: The refund articles are kept in a different file from the gift one
choices.why: All 40 articles are in data/help.jsonl, and the second grep counted 8 lines that mention a refund in that same file.

choices.text: grep ignores the body of each line and reads only the titles
choices.why: grep reads whole lines, and the gift article matched on its body: the words money back are in its last sentence.

choices.text: The search needed to be case-sensitive to find them
choices.why: -i makes it case-insensitive, which can only find more lines. Case was never the problem; the words were.

prompt: A shop keeps a hand-written list of synonyms for its search: refund = money back, parcel = box. A customer types 'the box never showed up'. What is the list still missing?
hint: The article's title is A parcel marked as delivered that never arrived.

choices.text: A synonym for parcel, since box is the customer's word for it
choices.why: The list already has parcel = box. The problem is the rest of the sentence.

choices.text: That showed up and arrived name one event
choices.why: Right. A synonym list works word by word; the match here is between two phrasings of an event, which is a matter of meaning, and it is what an embedding compares.

choices.text: Stemming, so that arrived matches arrive
choices.why: Stemming would let arrive match arrived, but the customer wrote neither. It cannot connect showed up to arrived.

choices.text: Spelling correction for showed
choices.why: Nothing is misspelt. Both phrasings are correct English that share no words.

prompt: `first.py` printed `(384,) float32`. What would it print for a three-paragraph article instead of a four-word title?
hint: The 384 belongs to something other than the text.

choices.text: A bigger shape
choices.why: The vector does not grow with the text. That would make two texts of different lengths impossible to compare coordinate by coordinate.

choices.text: (384,) float32 again
choices.why: Right. The dimension is a property of the model. Every text that goes through all-MiniLM-L6-v2 comes out as 384 numbers.

choices.text: Several vectors of 384, one per paragraph
choices.why: embed returns one vector per text it is given. A program could split the article into paragraphs first, as lesson 3 does, but that is a choice made before the model.

choices.text: An error, because the model reads only four words
choices.why: The model reads up to 256 word pieces. A three-paragraph article fits, and lesson 9 shows what happens past the limit.

prompt: The first coordinate of the refund title's vector is -0.0865. What does that number tell you about the title?
hint: Where does the section say the meaning lives?

choices.text: Nothing nameable; the meaning is in the whole vector
choices.why: Right. The information is spread over all 384 coordinates, and it shows up when the vector is compared with other vectors from the same model.

choices.text: That the title is slightly negative in tone, since the number is below zero
choices.why: No coordinate is a sentiment score. The sign of one number among 384 means nothing taken alone.

choices.text: How strongly the title is about money
choices.why: The model was never told what each coordinate should measure, and none of them lines up with a topic you could name.

choices.text: The position of the word refund in the model's own vocabulary
choices.why: Vocabulary positions are whole numbers used inside the tokeniser. The vector holds the result of the model's arithmetic, not an index.

prompt: A model returns vectors of 768 dimensions as float32. How many bytes does one vector take?
hint: A float32 is four bytes.

prompt: Marginalia embeds 10,000 articles with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and keeps the vectors as float32. How many megabytes is that, counting a megabyte as 1,000,000 bytes and nothing but the vectors?
hint: One vector is the 1,536 bytes first.py printed.

prompt: Vectors for the help centre were computed in January and stored. In June the same model, at the same version, embeds a new question. Can the question be compared with the stored vectors?
hint: Is there anything random in the model when it runs?

choices.text: Only if the stored vectors are computed again on the same day as the question
choices.why: The model has no randomness at inference: the January vectors are exactly what it would produce in June.

choices.text: Yes: the same text through the same model gives the same vector
choices.why: Right. That is what makes it possible to compute a document's vector once and keep it. It holds for as long as the model does not change.

choices.text: No, embeddings expire after a few months
choices.why: Nothing in a vector ages. What breaks a stored vector is a change of model, not the passing of time.

choices.text: Yes, but only for questions of exactly the same length
choices.why: Every text gives 384 numbers whatever its length, so length never stops a comparison.

prompt: `near.py` scores articles with the dot product. Why is that the same as the cosine of the angle for this model?
hint: first.py printed one more line.

choices.text: Because the model returns exactly 384 numbers
choices.why: The dimension has nothing to do with it. What matters is the length of each vector.

choices.text: Each vector has length 1
choices.why: Right. The cosine is the dot product divided by both lengths, and dividing by 1 changes nothing. Lesson 2 builds the formula.

choices.text: Because NumPy's @ operator computes a cosine
choices.why: @ computes a plain dot product. It equals the cosine here only because of something about the vectors.

choices.text: Because the texts being compared are all in English
choices.why: The language of the text has no bearing on the arithmetic between two vectors.

prompt: In `near.py`, the article about returning a gift scored 0.446 and the article that answers the question scored 0.438. What does that show?
hint: What does the score measure?

choices.text: The program has a bug that mixes up the order of the ids before printing
choices.why: The program pairs each score with its own id before sorting. The order is what the model computed.

choices.text: Embeddings rank by closeness of meaning, and a gift returned for money is close
choices.why: Right. The score says how near two texts are in meaning, not which one answers. Lesson 3 measures how often the best answer lands first and how often in the top three.

choices.text: The model prefers shorter articles and pushes the long ones down
choices.why: Nothing in the output connects score with length, and the gift article is not the shortest of the six.

choices.text: Keyword search is better than embeddings for this question
choices.why: Keyword search found only the gift article. The embedding put all four money-back articles above the unrelated ones.

prompt: Order these articles as `near.py` ranked them against 'how do I get my money back', from the highest score to the lowest.
hint: The four money-back articles came first, and the gift article led them.
trap: Two-step sign-in is not last: Delivery times and costs scored -0.016, below it.

prompt: In the two-axis picture, two article titles look very close together. What can you conclude about their vectors?
hint: How much of the variance did the two axes keep?

choices.text: That they are close in 384 dimensions too, since a projection keeps distances
choices.why: A projection to two axes keeps only part of the spread, 0.317 of the variance here. Points close on paper can be further apart in the full space.

choices.text: Nothing certain: compute their dot product to know
choices.why: Right. The picture shows that a structure exists, and the real comparison is the score between the two vectors.

choices.text: That they belong to the same category
choices.why: Categories tend to group, but Damaged books on arrival sits away from its own category. Position in the picture is not a label.

choices.text: That one of them is a duplicate
choices.why: Two different texts can be near in meaning without being copies, and the picture cannot even guarantee they are near.

prompt: How did all-MiniLM-L6-v2 come to place 'money back' near 'refund'?
hint: Contrastive.

choices.text: Its authors gave it a dictionary of synonyms to follow
choices.why: No list of synonyms went into it. That is the hand-kept list the first section said embeddings replace.

choices.text: Training on matching pairs pulled them close
choices.why: Right. The two phrasings kept turning up on both sides of matching pairs, so training placed them near each other.

choices.text: It looks up the definitions of both words each time it runs
choices.why: The model looks nothing up when it runs. Everything it knows was fixed in its weights during training.

choices.text: It counts how often the two words appear in the help centre
choices.why: The model never saw Marginalia's articles before this lesson. It brings what it learned to them.

prompt: Training that pulls the vectors of matching pairs together and pushes them away from the other texts in the batch is called ___ training.
hint: Every step sets one right partner against many wrong ones.

prompt: WordLlama scored 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' as 1.0. Why is that the expected result for this model and not a malfunction?
hint: Look at the token list order.py printed.

choices.text: Same five tokens; an average ignores order
choices.why: Right. A static model looks each token up and averages, and an average does not depend on order.

choices.text: WordLlama rounds every score above 0.99 to 1.0
choices.why: The 1.0 is exact: the two vectors are identical, so there is nothing to round.

choices.text: Its vectors have only 256 dimensions, too few to tell them apart
choices.why: Fewer dimensions can blur meaning, but they cannot make two different vectors identical. The cause is how the vector is built.

choices.text: It reads only the first word of each sentence
choices.why: It reads all five tokens; the last line of the output lists them. It just averages them.

prompt: A model that gives each token one fixed vector, whatever surrounds it, and averages them is called a ___ model.
hint: The opposite of contextual.

prompt: Put in order what happens inside all-MiniLM-L6-v2 between a text and its vector.
hint: The average comes late, and the division by the length comes last.
items: Split the text into word pieces
Give each piece a starting vector
Run six layers in which every piece looks at the others
Divide by the length so it is 1
trap: The average is not taken before the layers: that would be a static model. The layers work on the pieces one by one, and only their results are averaged.

prompt: 'I want a refund' and 'I do not want a refund' scored 0.892. A support team wants to route only the messages that ask for a refund. What should it conclude?
hint: What does an embedding capture best?

choices.text: A similarity threshold set above 0.9 will separate the two kinds of message
choices.why: The negated sentence scored 0.892 and the paraphrase scored 0.627. No threshold puts the paraphrase in and the negation out.

choices.text: Use a different similarity formula
choices.why: The vectors themselves are close; any formula over them inherits that. The limit is in what the model encoded.

choices.text: Similarity tracks the subject, not the assertion; a classifier must decide
choices.why: Right. Negation changes what a sentence says while leaving its subject alone. Lesson 4 trains a classifier for exactly this kind of decision.

choices.text: Translate the messages into Portuguese before embedding them
choices.why: This model scores Portuguese as unrelated to English, so translation would make matters worse, and it does nothing about negation.

prompt: 'How to return a book' against 'Como devolver um livro' scored -0.015 with all-MiniLM-L6-v2. What would bring the two titles close together?
hint: The cause is what the model was trained on.

choices.text: A multilingual model
choices.why: Right. This model was trained on English pairs, and a model trained on pairs across languages would place a title and its translation together.

choices.text: Normalising both vectors to length 1 before comparing
choices.why: They already have length 1. Normalising changes no direction, so the score would not move.

choices.text: Lower-casing the Portuguese title so the pieces match
choices.why: The tokeniser lower-cases everything already. The problem is that the model has no pairs for Portuguese.

choices.text: Adding more Portuguese articles to the help centre
choices.why: The model does not learn from the documents it embeds. Its vectors were fixed by training.

prompt: A team replaces all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with another model that also returns 384 numbers. What happens to the vectors already stored?
hint: Same dimension does not mean same space.

choices.text: They keep working, since the dimension matches
choices.why: A matching dimension only means the multiplication runs. The coordinates of one model have nothing to do with those of the other.

choices.text: They work for English texts and fail for the rest
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with it: every comparison between the two models' vectors is meaningless, in any language.

choices.text: Every one has to be embedded again
choices.why: Right. A vector only means something next to vectors from the same model. Lesson 18 prices that re-embedding.

choices.text: They need to be renormalised once, then they work
choices.why: Renormalising changes lengths, not directions. The directions belong to the old model and stay meaningless to the new one.

prompt: A vendor offers to store Marginalia's message vectors on its servers, saying that 'only numbers leave your systems, never the customers' words'. What is wrong with the argument?
hint: What did the 2023 paper on inversion do?

choices.text: Nothing; a vector cannot be turned back into any text at all
choices.why: Research on embedding inversion trained a model that rebuilt many short texts word for word from their vectors.

choices.text: The vectors are larger than the texts, so the transfer costs more
choices.why: They are larger, but that is a matter of cost. The argument is about what the vendor can learn, and size does not answer it.

choices.text: The vendor could only read the vectors with the same model
choices.why: The model is public, and an inversion model trained against it is exactly what the research built. Knowing the model makes recovery easier, not impossible.

choices.text: Vectors give away part of the text they came from, so they are personal data too
choices.why: Right. A vector of a customer's message is personal data like the message, and goes under the same rules about who reads it and how long it is kept.

prompt: Match each pair `limits.py` scored to what it showed.
hint: One pair is there as a control.

pairs.left: I want a refund / I do not want a refund
pairs.right: Opposite assertions about one subject score as close

pairs.left: How to return a book / Como devolver um livro
pairs.right: An English model treats Portuguese as unrelated

pairs.left: How to return a book / How to return a lamp
pairs.right: A different object, same action: middling score

pairs.left: I want a refund / Please give me my money back
pairs.right: The same request in other words

prompt: Marginalia stores the vector of every help article to search them next year. Which of these must be kept beside each vector for that to work? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what a vector cannot say about itself.

choices.text: Which model and version produced it
choices.why: Yes. Without it nobody knows which questions can be compared with the vector, or when it has to be recomputed.

choices.text: The article's id, to find the text again
choices.why: Yes. A search returns vectors, and a reader needs the article; the id is the join.

choices.text: The vector's length
choices.why: It can be computed from the vector at any time, and for this model it is always 1.

choices.text: The first coordinate on its own, as a summary
choices.why: One coordinate says nothing by itself; the meaning is in the whole vector.

prompt: Match each term to what it means in this lesson.
hint: Four terms, four definitions, one spare.

pairs.right: How many numbers a model returns for any text
Averages fixed token vectors, so order is lost
Lets the pieces adjust to each other before averaging
A flat picture that keeps part of the spread

right_distractors: A list of synonyms kept by hand

prompt: The number of values a model returns for every text, 384 for all-MiniLM-L6-v2, is called its ___.
hint: Lesson 2 is named after it.
